Activities

Last updated 17 October 2026

On this page
  • How an activity runs
  • Making one
  • The SDK (version 1)
  • A complete example
  • The built-in ones

Activities are small apps people use together in a voice channel: a game, a quiz, a shared toy. Someone in the call presses Activities in the call controls, picks one, and everyone else in the call sees "Alex started Four in a row — Join". The activity opens in the call's big spot for everyone who joins.

Iskra comes with three: Draw & guess, Quiz and Four in a row. A server's admins can add their own in Server settings → Activities. This page is about making one.

The wire protocol (what the server checks and relays) is in PROTOCOL.md → Activities.

How an activity runs#

  • It's a web page in a sealed frame. It has no network at all: no fetch, XHR, WebSocket, WebRTC, images or fonts from elsewhere, forms, pop-ups or navigation. It can use its own files, data: and blob: URLs, canvas, audio from its own files, and state in memory (it gets an opaque origin: no cookies, localStorage or IndexedDB).
  • It talks only to Iskra, through the SDK below. Iskra sends what it says to everyone playing, through your server, in the same order for everyone (yourself included). Nothing it sends is stored, apart from one snapshot for people who join late, kept in the server's memory until the activity ends.
  • Listeners watch. People who may only listen in a voice channel can join an activity there and see everything, but what they send is refused.
  • No filters. Activity messages aren't chat: AutoMod and word filters don't check them. Show other players' text with care (and never as HTML).
  • It never sees accounts. Players are an id that is only valid inside this activity session, and a display name.
  • Where it runs: activities added to a server run in the Iskra desktop app, which runs them in a wall where nothing can reach the network. Browsers can't be made that tight (a page script can always reach the internet through WebRTC in a child frame), so browsers and the phone apps list your activity but don't run it, and say it runs in the desktop app. The built-in activities run everywhere: they're part of Iskra.
  • Not in encrypted voice channels: the server relays what activities send, so they're off there.

Making one#

A zip (up to 5 MB, 200 files, 10 MB unpacked) with at least these two files at the top (or inside one folder):

my-activity.zip
├── manifest.json
├── index.html
├── game.js
└── icon.png

manifest.json:

JSON
{
  "name": "Snake duel",
  "description": "Two snakes, one screen.",
  "icon": "icon.png",
  "minPlayers": 2,
  "maxPlayers": 4,
  "version": "1.0",
  "sdk": 1
}

Only name (1–40 characters) is required. description is up to 200 characters, version up to 20, players 1–25.

Rules for the files:

  • File names use A–Z a–z 0–9 _ . -, don't start with a dot, and sit at most 8 folders deep.
  • Allowed types: html htm js mjs css json txt svg png jpg jpeg gif webp ico avif woff woff2 ttf otf mp3 ogg oga wav m4a opus. Text files must be UTF-8.
  • One page: index.html is the activity. It can't navigate to another page.
  • Classic scripts: use <script src="game.js"> or inline <script>, not type="module" (module scripts need CORS, which a sealed frame's origin doesn't get). Bundle with any tool into one IIFE file.
  • Only .html pages run scripts. Any other file (an SVG opened on its own, say) is served with scripts off.
  • Iskra's server puts two scripts in front of your page: one that removes WebRTC, and the SDK, which defines window.iskra. You don't need to include anything.

Upload the zip in Server settings → Activities → Add an activity. The server checks every file; anything outside the rules refuses the whole zip, with the reason.

The SDK (version 1)#

JavaScript
const init = await iskra.ready()
// init.me       { id, name }              you, in this activity
// init.players  [{ id, name }, …]         everyone in it, longest-in first
// init.state    the snapshot, or null     what the activity looked like when you joined
// init.locale   'en', 'sv', …             the player's language
// init.theme    { scheme: 'dark' | 'light', colors: { bg, surface, surface2, border, text, muted, accent, green, red, amber } }

iskra.on('message', (data, from, seq) => { … })   // every message, yours too, in the same order for everyone
iskra.on('players', (players) => { … })           // someone joined or left
iskra.on('end', () => { … })                      // the activity is ending

iskra.send(data)       // any JSON, up to 8 KB, to everyone playing
iskra.setState(state)  // a snapshot (any JSON, up to 48 KB) for people who join later
iskra.end()            // ends it for everyone (if you may), else closes it for you

iskra.me               // { id, name }
iskra.players          // [{ id, name }]
iskra.host             // the id of whoever has been in longest

Call iskra.ready() first and register your message listener right after it resolves: messages that arrive before anyone listens are held and handed over in order.

Keeping everyone in step#

The easy way to build a multiplayer activity on this SDK:

  1. Keep all shared state in one object.
  2. Write apply(state, data, from): a pure function that returns the next state for a message (or the same state when the message isn't valid: out of turn, malformed, from someone who may not do that). Check everything: other players' apps send whatever they like.
  3. To do anything, iskra.send() a message, and change the state only in your message listener. Every player applies the same messages in the same order, so everyone ends up in the same state, with no host needed.
  4. Let iskra.host call iskra.setState(state) after changes (Iskra sends at most one snapshot every 1.5 s, the latest wins). Someone who joins gets that snapshot as init.state, then every message after it.

Things only one player's app should know (a word to draw, a quiz's answers) stay in that app until it reveals them in a message. Never trust data as HTML: put text in with textContent.

Limits#
A message 8 KB of JSON; 10 a second (20 in a burst) per player; the whole session relays up to 256 KB a second, counted once per player it reaches
A snapshot 48 KB of JSON; at most one every 1.5 s
Players 25 at once, or your manifest's maxPlayers if fewer
Messages kept for late joiners those since the last snapshot, up to 300 and 256 KB

The messages underneath#

If you'd rather not use the helper: the SDK posts { iskra: 1, type: 'ready' | 'send' | 'state' | 'end', … } to window.parent (in the desktop app's wall, where there is no parent, it writes them as console lines starting with \u2063iskra-activity:), and receives { iskra: 1, type: 'init' | 'players' | 'message' | 'ended', … } as message events. See protocol/activity-sdk.js; the app checks every message (client/src/state/activityHost.ts).

A complete example#

index.html:

HTML
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <button id="go">Press me</button>
  <ol id="log"></ol>
  <script src="game.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

game.js:

JavaScript
;(async () => {
  const init = await iskra.ready()
  let state = init.state ?? { presses: [] }
  const names = new Map(init.players.map((p) => [p.id, p.name]))
  iskra.on('players', (players) => players.forEach((p) => names.set(p.id, p.name)))

  const render = () => {
    const log = document.getElementById('log')
    log.replaceChildren(...state.presses.map((id) => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: names.get(id) ?? 'Someone' })))
  }

  iskra.on('message', (data, from) => {
    if (data?.t !== 'press' || state.presses.length >= 50) return
    state = { presses: [...state.presses, from] }
    render()
    if (iskra.host === iskra.me.id) iskra.setState(state)
  })

  document.getElementById('go').onclick = () => iskra.send({ t: 'press' })
  render()
})()

Zip index.html, game.js and a manifest.json with a name, and add it to your server.

The built-in ones#

client/src/activities/ holds the three built-ins, written against the same SDK: each is a reducer (logic.ts, unit tested) and a small DOM view (main.ts). client/activities.vite.ts builds each into one self-contained HTML file.
